studies.title: He Has Not Left You
studies.meaning: Two oaths by times of day, and then a denial of two specific things: your Lord has not taken leave of you, and has not turned against you. Both are answers to a fear rather than statements of doctrine. Then three past facts, each a rescue, phrased as questions. Then three instructions built from those facts, in the same order: the orphan, the one who asks, and the blessing that is to be spoken about.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The sources report the occasion with reasonable agreement. Revelation had paused for a period, and people in Mecca had begun to say that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had been abandoned. The reports differ over how long the pause lasted, from days to weeks. The surah answers the taunt directly, and its first word is an oath by the light of morning.

keyTerms.note: The word for mid-morning, after sunrise and before noon, when the light is full and the day has not yet turned hot. It names the best hour of an Arabian day, and the surah is named after it.
The verb used for a farewell between people who are parting deliberately, not for neglect. Denying it answers a specific accusation: not that God forgot, but that He said goodbye.
Used of a night that has become calm and of the sea when it stops moving. The oath pairs a bright hour with a quiet one, which is the emotional range the surah is addressing.
A participle covering a beggar and anyone making a request, including a question. Early scholars take both, so the instruction runs to the person asking for money and the person asking to be taught.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An orphan in Mecca had no protector, in a society built entirely on protection. Property could be taken and marriages arranged badly, and there was no authority to appeal to. A boy's future depended on which uncle took him in. The surah reminds its listener of that state, and then, in the same breath, hands him a rule about how to treat someone still in it.
studies.didYouKnow: The second half of the surah answers the first half item by item, though not in the same sequence. Found orphaned, so do not oppress the orphan; found in need, so do not turn away the one who asks; found without direction and guided, so speak about what you were given. Three rescues and three instructions, matched one to one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comfort offered is not a promise about the future first. It is a review of the past. Three things that already happened are produced as evidence, so the argument can be checked by memory rather than by faith. Then the surah does something unexpected with that comfort. It turns it into a duty. Having been sheltered, do not crush. Having been given, do not turn anyone away.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same list of past favours in the surah immediately after, in the same questioning form.
Names the failure this surah's instruction guards against, someone who pushes an orphan away.
Gives the same refusal to read a long silence as abandonment, spoken by a father waiting for news.

studies.applyIt: Write down three times you were helped when you could not have arranged it yourself. Not general gratitude, three specific occasions with dates if you can. Then pick one person currently in the position you were in during any of the three, and do the smallest useful thing for them. That is the shape of this surah in one afternoon.
studies.explainEasier: God tells his messenger that he has not left him and has not forgotten him. He reminds him that he was an orphan and was taken in, was lost and was guided, was poor and was given enough. Then he tells him to be kind to orphans.
